item.title: AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes After Eight Years at 15
item.description:
AWS has raised the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes in all commercial regions, with no opt-in and no new pricing. The limit had stood since 2018. AWS's post lists the costs: twice the concurrency at the same request rate, three-hour SQS visibility timeouts, and Kafka mappings that must be recreated. Practitioners welcome it and ask what belongs elsewhere.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

item.title: How to choose a secure PDF solution for your business
item.description:
AI is changing the economics and speed of cyberattacks. In September 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported that a three-person security research team used Anthropic’s Claude to chain together software flaws and reach OpenAI’s internal code systems. The researchers were white-hat testers working through a bug-bounty program, and the full path from a newly found bug to access took under three days. The lesson is sobering: work that once required a well-resourced team can increasingly be done by a few people using off-the-shelf AI. And this shift is showing up at scale: CrowdStrike reported that AI-driven adversary activity rose 89% year over year, and the fastest intrusion it recorded spread across a network in 27 seconds. As AI makes it faster and cheaper to find vulnerabilities and turn them into working attacks, enterprises have less time to detect, contain, and respond to threats.

As the widely adopted format for information exchange, the PDF can also be one of the largest attack surfaces in the enterprise. Trillions of PDFs are in circulation, carrying documents that organizations run on: contracts, financial records, board materials, patient files, and government forms. Every day employees open files that arrive from outside the organization: an emailed invoice, a signed contract, a resume, a statement from a vendor. Any one of them can carry malware, and AI has sharply lowered the cost of creating it. The most reliable defense is not to keep playing catch-up after each new exploit is discovered, but to contain the threat at its foundation, in the desktop software that opens the file. That software is a core part of your security perimeter, and it deserves the same scrutiny you already apply to operating systems, browsers, and collaboration tools.

What to look for in a secure PDF solution.

When evaluating a PDF solution, organizations should look beyond features and price and consider four security requirements that apply to every vendor.

1. Containment: Can it prevent a malicious file from compromising your system or network?

Untrusted files enter the organization constantly through email, web downloads, shared drives, and vendor portals, and any one of them can be crafted to exploit the very application that opens it. That’s why most modern browsers and other applications that routinely process untrusted content use sandboxing as a first line of defense.

A sandbox creates an operating-system-enforced boundary around the application that restricts direct access to the file system, the network, and other applications, so that even a successful exploit is contained and cannot spread. Any action that needs to cross that boundary, such as saving a file, should be mediated by a small, tightly controlled broker with strictly validated permissions. The attack surface is now reduced to this tiny broker that can be tightly audited and secured. For this protection to be effective, sandboxing should be enabled by default, not an option an administrator has to discover and switch on.

2. Detection coverage: Will your security tools detect threats targeting your PDF solution?

Antivirus products, file scanners, and other security tools help identify malicious PDFs before they can do harm. To analyze a suspicious PDF, some security tools open it in a controlled environment and observe how it behaves. But an attack designed to exploit one PDF application may not activate when the file is opened in another. If the security tool doesn’t analyze the file using the application the attack was designed to target, the malicious behavior can go undetected.

That’s why the PDF solution an organization chooses can affect more than its ability to contain an attack. Organizations should also consider whether the security tools they rely on routinely test against that PDF solution, helping identify threats specifically designed to exploit it.

3. Security program: How mature is the security program behind the software?

Software is never finished, so the software provider’s ongoing security program matters as much as the product functionality. Look for a dedicated security team and a secure development lifecycle that’s secure by design, embedding security controls at the beginning of development and includes threat modeling, code review, static and dynamic analysis, and continuous fuzzing. A strong program should provide transparency and invite external scrutiny through a public bug-bounty program and coordinated vulnerability disclosure, and it should publish the results of its security testing rather than a single summary. Increasingly, strong software providers also apply frontier AI models to help find and fix vulnerabilities in their code before it reaches customers — and adversaries.

4. Response speed: How quickly and predictably are vulnerabilities fixed?

The gap between a vulnerability being discovered and exploited is now measured in days, which makes the speed and predictability of fixes a critical security control. Look for a solution that follows a regular, published update cadence and is able to ship out-of-band emergency patches when a situation demands it. Updates should deploy across the whole environment – automatically in case auto-update is enabled and easy to deploy by admins for scenarios where auto-update is disabled by admins.

PDF solution evaluation criteria checklist

Use this checklist to assess any PDF solution before you buy or renew. Ask the provider to show evidence for each item.

1) CONTAINMENT: Can a malicious file reach and attack our file systems and network?

[ ] Opens untrusted files inside an OS-enforced sandbox,

[ ] Sandbox is on by default

[ ] Sandbox available on every platform we run (Windows, macOS)

[ ] Actions that leave the sandbox go through a minimal, permission-checked broker

[ ] A successful exploit still cannot reach the file system, network, or other apps

2) DETECTION COVERAGE: Can our scanners see threats built for this software?

[ ] Major analysis services (VirusTotal, CrowdStrike Falcon Sandbox, Joe Sandbox,

ANY.RUN, Palo Alto WildFire) analyze PDFs as they open in this software

[ ] Exploits targeting this software would be caught by our detection stack,

not only discovered on the endpoint after they run

3) VULNERABILITY RESPONSE: How fast and predictably are flaws fixed?

[ ] Published, regular patch cadence

[ ] Out-of-band emergency fixes with a stated timeframe

[ ] Silent auto-update, plus easy admin deployment (Intune, SCCM, Jamf) when it’s off

[ ] Vendor issues its own CVEs (is a CNA), not reliant on third parties

4) SECURITY PROGRAM: Is security a serious, ongoing investment?

[ ] Dedicated product-security team and secure development lifecycle

(threat modeling, code review, static/dynamic analysis, fuzzing)

[ ] Public bug-bounty program and coordinated vulnerability disclosure

[ ] Publishes security bulletins and testing results, including internal findings

[ ] Applies AI to find and fix flaws in its own code before release

[ ] 24/7 incident response with a documented process

How Adobe Acrobat measures up

Acrobat was built with these four requirements in mind, combining containment by default with broad security ecosystem coverage, a mature security program, and a predictable approach to vulnerability response. These capabilities can vary across PDF solutions, making them important factors to evaluate when choosing one.

Containment, by default

Acrobat processes every file inside a sandbox, the operating-system-enforced boundary described above. Almost all of its work, including parsing and rendering the file, happens inside that sandbox. When Acrobat needs to act outside it, the request passes through a small broker process that is the only component with real permissions, and every request is validated. If a malicious file exploits a vulnerability, the exploit is trapped inside the boundary and prevented from reaching your file system, your network, or your other applications. Containment is on by default. PDF applications without this type of sandbox architecture may process files with broader system permissions, increasing the potential impact if a vulnerability is successfully exploited.

How sandboxing helps contain a malicious file: Acrobat processes untrusted content within an OS-enforced boundary while a trusted broker mediates requests that require access outside the sandbox.

Detection across the security ecosystem

Because Acrobat is one of the most widely used PDF applications in the world, the sandboxes and scanning engines inside antivirus and threat-analysis tools typically open a PDF in Acrobat and watch how it behaves. A file crafted to exploit a different PDF product often does nothing in Acrobat, so those scanners could clear it, and it detonates only when it reaches a machine running the software it was built for. Independent researchers have documented this pattern. The software you choose affects not just how well it contains a threat, but whether your broader security stack can see the threat at all.

A mature, transparent security program

Acrobat is backed by a dedicated, full-time security team and a secure development lifecycle: threat modeling, code review, static analysis, penetration testing, and continuous fuzzing with memory and race-condition sanitizers. Adobe now applies frontier AI to Acrobat’s own code before it ships. Acrobat runs a bug-bounty program that turns independent researchers into an extension of the team, practices coordinated disclosure, and publishes the results of its security testing, including internal findings, not just an outside summary. A 24/7 incident response team stands behind Acrobat, and Adobe has been recognized by Microsoft as its Security ISV of the Year.

Fast, predictable fixes

Adobe aligns with the secure-by-design and secure-by-default expectations set out by government cybersecurity agencies. Security updates ship on a regular, predictable cadence, with out-of-band emergency fixes when a situation calls for it, and they install quietly across an organization with no action required from users and no manual redeployment by administrators. Protection arrives without waiting on anyone.

Across all four requirements — from containment and detection coverage to security engineering and vulnerability response — Acrobat brings a comprehensive approach to PDF security. Adobe’s commitment to the full combination is one reason organizations of all sizes choose Acrobat for their most important document work.

The software that opens your documents deserves the same scrutiny as the software that opens the internet.

Every organization depends on documents, and increasingly every document is a file that someone outside your organization could use to reach inside it. As AI accelerates both attackers and defenders, the safest starting point is software that contains threats by design, is backed by a serious and transparent security program, and fixes issues quickly. When you evaluate an enterprise PDF solution, bring your IT and security teams into the decision, and hold every vendor to the four requirements above. The right answers protect far more than a document. They protect everything your documents can reach.

To learn more about Adobe’s approach to product security, explore the rest of this security series or visit the Adobe Trust Center.

item.title: Rethinking resilience in a dynamic digital world
item.description:
Organisations are being forced to reconsider what cyber resilience means in the age of AI. As technologies and threats evolve, leading organisations recognise that resilience depends on their ability to keep pace and adapt to this changing landscape, often in real time.

Findings from PwC’s “2027 Global Digital Trust Insights” survey reveal how the changing nature of cyber risk is testing organisations’ preparedness, from their ability to counter emerging threats to the effectiveness of their security operations and leadership.

A complex risk and threat landscape

Enterprise AI systems are emerging as a major cyber vulnerability. Half of the surveyed security leaders identified attacks targeting AI systems as one of their biggest preparedness gaps. The concern is growing as frontier AI models become capable of finding and exploiting previously unknown software vulnerabilities with minimal human intervention.

Geopolitical volatility is also forcing businesses to reconsider risks beyond their immediate control. Half of the respondents are changing their third-party and supply chain risk management strategies in response.

Looking further ahead, quantum computing presents another challenge. Only 21% are implementing quantum-resistant security measures, and 49% are not implementing them or have no planned activity.

The gap between investment and operational preparedness

Cybersecurity budgets are set to continue increasing, with 84% of security and finance leaders expecting them to grow in 2027. Yet only 39% of security, risk and operations leaders have fully integrated operational continuity plans that address cyber risks.

“It’s not purely about how much you’re investing. It’s really about thinking through how you deal with that level of disruption,” says James Rashleigh, EMEA Cyber Leader, PwC UK.

That means looking beyond protection to a more fundamental question: if a critical part of the organisation’s operations fails, how quickly can the business recover?

Data protection exposes another weakness. Organisations have implemented an average of just three of seven key data risk measures identified in the survey. Greater cybersecurity spending will deliver resilience only if it strengthens these underlying capabilities.

AI strengthens cyber defences

AI is helping organisations detect threats and respond to potential attacks more quickly, with threat detection and alerting emerging as the leading applications for the technology in cybersecurity. However, organisations remain cautious about allowing AI agents to act independently.

Only 22% would authorise AI agents to activate cyber defences without human approval, and 55% cite concerns about the technology’s reliability and maturity as a barrier to greater autonomy.

Extending cyber capabilities through managed services

As cybersecurity becomes more complex, organisations are turning to external specialists for additional support. AI (53%) and cloud security (49%) lead security leaders’ priorities for managed services, followed by data protection and trust (42%) and threat management (39%) over the coming year.

Conclusion: turning investment into resilience

Cyber resilience will depend on how effectively organisations turn investment into stronger foundations and the ability to respond when disruption strikes. PwC’s findings identify four priorities:

  • Strengthen governance: Make cyber risk part of business decisions, with clear accountability.
  • Build operational resilience: Identify essential services, test recovery plans and understand third-party dependencies.
  • Secure data and AI: Address weaknesses in data protection before giving AI agents greater responsibility.
  • Align security with business value: Consider cyber risk from the outset when investing in technology and developing new services.

Ultimately, cyber resilience will be measured by an organisation’s ability to withstand disruption and adapt to whatever comes next.

item.title: Your AI incident clock is already running. The US-China channel hasn’t said what starts it
item.description:
On November 19 in Shenzhen, China, Xi Jinping told Donald Trump that the two countries should coordinate on AI security risks and “ensure AI always remains under human control,” according to China’s Foreign Ministry readout. The next day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC the leaders had agreed to keep humans involved in any military decision AI makes. AI, he added, should not act on its own in major military actions. Neither government has published a text with those terms, and Beijing’s readout never mentions the military.

The fall summits also left the two governments with an agreed channel for AI incidents, and its vocabulary shows how much remains unsettled. The White House’s September fact sheet says the leaders agreed to call the technology “super intelligence” and to set up a channel for “SI incidents.” It defines neither term. China’s Commerce Ministry, quoted by state broadcaster CNR, says the two sides have established an “AI incident communication channel.” Beijing’s Shenzhen readout has Trump saying “super intelligence” and Xi saying “artificial intelligence.” No public announcement says what triggers a report.

Before the September summit, Bessent said the two sides still had to “agree on what the leading AI dangers are.” He offered uncontrollable agents, non-state actors and bioweapons as candidates. A list of dangers is not a trigger. Public health writes the trigger down. Under the International Health Regulations, a country assesses each event with a decision instrument in Annex 2 and notifies the World Health Organization within 24 hours of that assessment. The US-China channel has a phone line and no published Annex.

Enterprises face a sharper version of the same gap. A company that runs an AI service already answers to its regulators’ incident clocks, each with its own trigger, recipient and deadline. A public company has four business days after deciding a cybersecurity incident is material to file an SEC Form 8-K. A New York-regulated bank or insurer has 72 hours after determining an incident occurred to notify the state’s financial regulator, including incidents at its third-party service providers. A model that leaks data or an agent that breaks a production system can start those clocks.

Beijing already runs the clock

China’s incident rules show what a published national trigger looks like. Since November 1, 2025, measures from the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) have required companies that run networks or online services in China to grade each security incident they discover against four severity tiers. Reporting starts at “relatively major,” the second-lowest tier; one of its criteria is a 10-minute total outage of critical infrastructure. Critical infrastructure operators then report to their supervising department and the police within one hour, and other companies report to their provincial CAC office within four hours. When the cause or impact is still unclear, a company can file the basic facts first and supply the rest later. Each operator must also bind its security and maintenance vendors, by contract or similar means, to report what they detect. A written analysis follows within 30 days after the response ends. An AI service that leaks data or goes down falls under these rules like any other online service, including at a US company’s China subsidiary.

AI-specific layers sit on top, and they carry different legal weight. A practice guide from China’s cybersecurity standards committee, TC260, sets out how to classify and grade generative AI security incidents. Binding rules in force since July 15 add duties for AI companion services and expressly exclude customer service bots and work assistants that offer no sustained emotional interaction. An October 9 policy document from the Communist Party’s Central Committee and the State Council calls for AI monitoring, risk early warning and emergency response. On November 3, a National Development and Reform Commission official said Beijing will accelerate comprehensive AI legislation, and called on developers and operators to report incidents and vulnerabilities. Beijing has not yet published a draft, and the national legislature closed its November session without one.

America’s frontier AI clocks point at the developer

The US frontier AI laws add a second clock and attach it to the model maker. California’s SB 53 gives frontier developers 15 days from discovery to report a critical safety incident to the state Office of Emergency Services. New York’s RAISE Act gives large frontier developers 72 hours to report to a state office after they determine, or have reason to believe, that an incident occurred, starting in January 2027. Under both laws, a developer that finds an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury has 24 hours to notify law enforcement or a public safety agency. At the federal level, Trump called the accord he signed with tech executives on September 29 “morally binding,” but no law or regulation requires companies to follow it.

Both laws require developers to report incidents to a state agency. A background paper for an October 27 California Assembly oversight hearing notes that SB 53 does not require developers to notify individuals, businesses or organizations affected by a critical safety incident. Put the layers side by side, and the split I described in September reappears: different duties attach to different companies inside the same AI service. General cyber rules in both countries bind the company running the service. The frontier laws bind the company that built the model. A deployer can owe a regulator a report on a failure, but California’s law does not require the model provider to tell the deployer. A CIO who wants that notice has to put it in the contract.

Beijing’s machinery is no “drag and drop” template. Its reporting lines run to the CAC, which also polices online speech, and for critical infrastructure to the police. None of this is a case for importing China’s content controls. The transferable part is the structure underneath, the mechanism: a graded trigger, a clock, a first report allowed on incomplete facts, a duty that runs down the supply chain, and a record.

The next US-China AI dialogue will show whether the channel gets published triggers. If it does, CIOs gain a common reference point. If it does not, the duties that bind companies stay with each government’s own regulators.

Four decisions to make before your next AI incident

  1. A test, not a list. Start from the OECD’s published definitions of an AI incident and turn them into a short triage test. Did a model expose data without authorization? Did a model or agent act, or change a system of record, beyond its permissions? Did a model’s output or action harm a customer, an employee or the business? Did someone compromise a model, its weights or its tools? Name one owner who grades each yes by data sensitivity, affected functions and harm, and who can pull the service. When a support chatbot exposes customer records, that owner decides whether to report the exposure.
  2. Two clocks. Set one fast internal clock to detect, grade and escalate to security and legal, and route external filings by jurisdiction and regulator. Decide in advance who can authorize a first report on incomplete facts, so headquarters approval does not consume a subsidiary’s reporting window.
  3. Notice from vendors. Ask model providers, cloud hosts and AI vendors for incident notice that starts at credible detection, not at the end of their investigation. Specify what it must name: the affected model version, known impact, containment steps and the time of the next update. Treat a silent change in model behavior as a notice event, separate from a data breach. Large providers will not accept every clause, so log model calls through your own gateway and watch for failures yourself.
  4. A record. Keep a written analysis of every graded incident: cause, response, harm, accountability and fixes. Before short-lived logs roll over, capture what an outage ticket misses: the model version, system prompt, retrieved context, tool permissions and the actions the system took. Link each record to the AI model, vendor and permissions involved, so repeat failures surface as patterns before they become the next incident.

Washington and Beijing have agreed to tell each other about AI incidents. Before any regulator asks, a CIO needs to know what broke, who noticed, when the clock started and who signed the first report.

item.title: The AI invoice is a governance signal most CIOs are failing to read
item.description:
Generative AI has fundamentally rewritten the expectations around enterprise software development. With coding assistants dramatically accelerating output, most IT leaders naturally assume outsourced development costs should be plummeting.

Yet when the monthly invoice from your technology partners arrives, the figures often tell a different story: static costs in a time of hyper-accelerated coding.

This discrepancy isn’t necessarily a sign of misalignment or padded billing. Rather, it points to a profound and glaring issue in the advanced enterprise tech ecosystem: the fundamental nature of software engineering has changed. The effort (and therefore the cost) has migrated from writing code to governing it.

Your IT partner’s invoice now signals the complex reality of AI oversight.

Faster code, same bill

The speed is real. GitLab’s 2026 AI Accountability Report, a Harris Poll survey of 1,528 developers and technology buyers, found that 78% of organizations see code being written and committed faster. In the same survey, 85% agreed that the bottleneck has shifted from writing code to reviewing and validating it.

So, typing got cheaper, and everything after typing got heavier. Typing was never the expensive part anyway. Reading, testing, securing and owning the code is where most hours go, and AI hands those people more to read, not less.

The hidden governance tax inside your AI spend

The financial reality of the AI era is that a massive chunk of enterprise IT spend is now silently dedicated to AI governance, or worse, the manual labor required to compensate for a lack of it.

If your service provider lacks a mature framework to manage AI hallucinations, trace the provenance of AI-generated code and enforce security compliance natively, their developers must do it manually. Every time they pause to manually verify whether an AI agent introduced a security vulnerability, you absorb a hidden governance tax.

The data confirms that the broader market is still playing catch-up. Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise report highlights that only 21% of organizations actually have a mature AI governance framework in place. To stop absorbing the cost of operational growing pains, IT leaders have to change how they vet external teams.

What’s actually inside the AI bill now

Governance used to be a policy PDF and a quarterly meeting. Now it’s a working cost center, and it tends to show up in a handful of places.

 

Another dimension of this challenge is the quality of context available to AI systems. Artefact’s work on context engineering highlights how knowledge graphs, ontologies and decision histories can help enterprise AI agents interpret business information, apply relevant rules and produce more traceable outcomes. This makes the underlying data architecture an increasingly important part of AI governance, not just the model itself.

The line items nobody budgeted

  • Model and tool access controls, including who can use what, on which data
  • Code provenance and audit trails
  • Human review capacity, which is the scarcest resource on the list
  • Security, IP and data-handling checks on AI output
  • Agent inventory, permissions and retirement
  • Regulatory mapping for each use case

Why it keeps growing

Volume. Gartner expects the average global Fortune 500 enterprise to run more than 150,000 AI agents by 2028, up from fewer than 15 in 2025. In the same release, only 13% of organizations said they believe they have the right agent governance in place. Governance effort scales with what’s running, so a bill that’s already carrying it will carry more next year.

Skipping it doesn’t make it free. It just moves the cost to incident response, where it’s priced at the worst possible rate.

This is also where provider choice starts to matter. Delivery partners that treat governance as part of the build rather than a bolt-on. Digital engineering collaborators like Appinventiv scope it end-to-end, from model access and code provenance to review and audit trails.

As an official OpenAI Select Partner and Anthropic’s Claude Partner, the firm tends to put it on the estimate up front. You’ll pay for it either way. The difference is whether you see it coming.

Who owns the bill?

Deloitte surveyed 3,235 leaders and found only about one in five companies has a mature model for governing autonomous agents. Meanwhile, 78% of FinOps practices now report to the CTO or CIO. So, the cost question is landing on your desk whether or not the governance question has an owner. That mismatch is worth fixing before a renewal, not after one.

Invoice line items worth questioning

A few patterns worth checking next time an AI invoice lands on your desk:

The third row is the one to worry about. A silent governance line usually means the work isn’t happening, or it’s quietly eroding the agency’s margin until quality slips.

How governance costs shift by industry

Governance isn’t a flat percentage. A fintech and a retailer don’t pay the same toll, and the difference starts with who’s watching.

Fintech shows the pattern most clearly. The RBI’s FREE-AI committee, reporting in August 2025, made 26 recommendations for India’s financial sector, including a board-approved AI policy that sorts use cases by risk and keeps humans in the loop on medium and high-risk ones.

Translate that into delivery, and you get extra approval gates, documentation and audit evidence for every AI-touched change. Those hours show up as line items.

Europe offers a useful timing warning. The EU’s Digital Omnibus pushed high-risk AI Act obligations for standalone systems to December 2027, and for AI embedded in regulated products to August 2028. But transparency duties began applying on August 2, 2026. Deferred isn’t cancelled, so budget for it.

Here, the delivery partner’s track record also carries significant weight. Some companies include model access controls, code provenance and audit trails as standard delivery, so the sector-specific layer doesn’t land as a surprise change request.

What estimates should look like with AI in the build

Businesses now walk into scoping calls expecting a steep discount. The logic is simple: if AI writes the code, why pay for the hours? It’s a fair question and deserves a straight answer, not a defensive one.

The honest answer is reallocation. You pay less for output and more for assurance. A credible estimate shows both sides.

Expect the total to move less than the headline suggests, and expect it to shift between rows. That shift is the story. An IT partner who shows you a 40% cut with no governance line has either not thought it through or is planning to recover it in change requests.

DORA’s 2025 research supports this, saying AI amplifies whatever your engineering system already is. Strong foundations get faster. Weak ones get unstable faster.

Your next AI invoice could lead to major changes

Pull your latest delivery invoice and run a small test. Find the line that tells you who reviewed the AI-written code, who can trace it back to a model, and who picks up the phone when it misbehaves in production. If that takes more than 10 minutes, the saving you were promised is sitting in a queue you can’t see, and queues like that get cleared eventually, usually at incident rates.

Code is cheap to produce now. Trust still costs full price, and someone pays for it either way. The only decision left is whether you pay in the estimate, on purpose, or after an incident.

item.title: Ally Financial reinvents customer personas with agentic AI
item.description:
When the bottom line depends on robust, personalized digital experiences, anticipating how customers and prospects will respond to new services or offerings or to changes in existing customer journeys is paramount. For that, leading organizations turn to personas to help get in the mind of consumers as a means for tailoring customer experiences to their desires and needs.

At digital financial services company Ally Financial, UX designers and content teams have long used personas to help hone digital experiences.

Each persona used by Ally is backed by a hefty amount of research, including demographic, marketing, and proprietary data, so that Ally employees can be confident that they had pragmatic insights into the thoughts, feelings, and likely reactions of the various types of consumers who contact and interact with the bank.

Ally’s designers use personas to test whether digital features, tools, and content meet consumers where they are — a feat that requires knowing their varying relationships with money as well as other characteristics and behaviors. The goal, according to Ally officials, is to use personas to create best-in-class digital experiences for each and every consumer engaging with the firm.

But traditional persona operations have evident limits, and in 2024, Ally designers began to wonder whether recent AI advances could make their personas do more.

“We valued the existing personas, which were rich with insights but were static, meaning designers could not engage and interact with them; designers could only apply them,” says Lizzie Pope, director of UX design. “And we were hearing about agentic AI and thought we could make these personas more interactive. So we asked, ‘Do we have an opportunity from an emerging tech perspective to interact with these personas more.’”

Enter the agent persona era

Ally technologists seized on this idea and transformed the company’s static customer personas into six distinct AI agent personas, each encoded with the financial backgrounds, goals, characteristics, values, device habits, financial relationships, and trusted brands characteristic of Ally’s 11 million-plus customers.

“What we wanted [these agent personas to do] is show how this person would behave in a given situation and to show what their reactions would be,” says Harish Naik, senior director lead and head of marketing tech and digital platforms at Ally.

Pope adds, “The idea was to have a persona that could react, providing real-time feedback, so designers wouldn’t have to imagine [how a customer would respond to a digital experience]. The designers would instantly get real responses, so when we go into human testing, we’re that much more confident.”

The agentic AI personas launched fully in the last quarter of 2025 after 16 months of development and pilots, under the leadership of then Chief Information, Data, and Digital Officer Sathish Muthukrishnan. Muthukrishnan left Ally in August 2026. The company’s new chief information and data officer is Mark Mathewson.

Ally already had a long history of using AI by the time it undertook building agentic AI personas, having used machine learning for years and implementing generative AI and large language models over the past several years. However, the persona initiative was its first foray into agentic AI, earning the company a 2026 CIO 100 Award for innovation and leadership.

Naik acknowledges the challenge that came with that. “This was a stretch goal we embarked on,” he says, noting that promising early results propelled the initiative forward. “It started with a proof of concept and moved to production pilot after going through approvals and governance.”

Naik and his team built the agentic AI personas on Ally.ai, a proprietary, cloud-based platform Ally launched in 2023 that has the functionality of traditional and generative AI tools, including foundational models, along with the specialized human touch and data security protections essential for a financial services company.

Having that platform in place enabled Ally’s technologists to move faster in launching the agentic AI personas, Naik explains, because they could leverage existing security controls, standards, guardrails, and APIs rather than create them from scratch.

Naik’s team also leveraged LangChain, an open-source orchestration framework for Python and JavaScript designed to help developers build LLM-powered applications, and LangGraph, an open-source, low-level orchestration framework and runtime built by LangChain to create stateful, multistep, and multi-agent AI workflows.

Tackling agentic AI’s shifting challenges

There were, of course, challenges in developing and using the agentic AI personas.

Safeguarding customer data was one. Ally implemented security, privacy, and governance safeguards, and it built them into its Ally.ai platform to prevent sharing any personally identifiable information (PII) with AI applications or LLMs.

Ensuring ethical, responsible AI use was the other top challenge. To address that, Ally stuck with one of its core AI principles of maintaining human involvement in all use cases; in the case of personas, feedback is delivered directly to the user in a chat format and then reviewed and incorporated by humans before further testing; humans also remain the final decision-makers.

Additionally, centralized observability via Ally.ai Observer Services provides holistic insights and explainability. Naik says the agentic AI framework used for the personas stores questions and responses, delivering the visibility needed to ensure trustworthiness and system resiliency.

Furthermore, Ally’s internal tech team and its UX designers worked through multiple rounds of testing, tweaking, and optimizing to ensure responses from the personas were accurate, reliable, and trustworthy.

Now, when Ally builds new digital products, designers use an interface to interact with the personas, enabling them to test how differing customer types will respond to digital content, features, and tools and — more critically — giving them real-time feedback so they can rapidly iterate, Pope explains.

The designers select one or more personas and layer in modifiers — Naik’s team built modifiers into the six core personas, creating a higher number of permutations. They then observe how each persona interacts with the digital product being tested, with the agents providing feedback.

Building on persona success

Designers still test with humans, Pope adds, but using the agentic AI personas enables designers to bring digital products that are more refined and closer to perfected to that final testing step than what they could achieve using static personas previously.

The agentic AI personas delivered value from launch, according to Ally officials, helping to ensure content and experiences are optimized for real customer needs, improving time-to-market for new digital experiences, boosting efficiency, and reducing costs.

For example, designers used an interactive persona agent to get feedback on how Ally reps could de-escalate the stress of starting to invest with certain details or callouts earlier in their conversion with customers. And they used an interactive persona to improve the content for an Ally.com automated investing product page after hearing from the agent that the page didn’t share enough about Ally’s portfolio types.

Buoyed by such success, Ally’s tech team is piloting employee personas that the HR department could use to better understand how employees would respond to employment issues, such as benefit options or internal information. And it’s evaluating dealer personas, which could be used to test digital products that serve auto dealers.

item.title: Changing the engine while flying: How to turn AI productivity gains into business transformation
item.description:
I’ve seen plenty of companies roll out copilots and AI assistants and expect individual productivity gains to translate into enterprise-level results. But it doesn’t usually work that way. Those gains, while real, almost always fall short of expectations when token costs, implementation expenses and existing process inefficiencies eat into the returns.

The underlying problem with this approach? Expecting transformational results without fundamentally changing how the work gets done.

Even as leaders are giving employees more powerful tools, they’re leaving the processes, organizational structures and operating assumptions surrounding those employees largely untouched. That’s making topical improvements, not undertaking a deep-tissue transformation.

Most of the leaders I hear from know that AI’s potential is much greater than the returns they’re seeing. But if they want to bridge that gap, they need to rethink what they’re trying to optimize and what meaningful AI ROI actually looks like.

Why AI productivity gains don’t translate into business value

Most enterprises tend to approach AI as an additive technology. Give employees access, provide training and let them use AI to perform existing tasks faster. And faster is better, right? Not necessarily. This approach mostly preserves the underlying workflow, including handoffs, functional silos, duplicated effort and unnecessary steps.

Our research shows that increasing the productivity of individual tasks increases the waiting time between tasks and does not reduce the overall lead time of a value stream. And individual productivity gains don’t automatically lower costs, accelerate delivery or create capacity for innovation. In essence, the organization is becoming more efficient at executing tasks that shouldn’t even exist in their current form.

This is also where the financial case breaks down, as incremental productivity gains are offset by AI token costs, making the economics of scaling that pilot less compelling. After all, a pilot that produces only modest improvements doesn’t justify the expense and complexity of deploying AI across thousands of employees.

Meanwhile, a broader drawback of this approach becomes clear. Measuring ROI primarily through things like tool adoption, access, usage and individual productivity obscures the larger economic opportunity of AI: Fundamentally redesigning workflows to transform incremental gains into exponential improvements of 5x or even 10x.

In many of the successful software development transformations I’ve worked on, for example, the organizations haven’t just given their people tools to speed up their existing work. They’ve used AI to combine previously separate phases, automate pre- and post-development activities and eliminate steps that no longer add value.

These changes have created opportunities to reduce operational costs and redirect resources toward innovation and business growth. That’s where real ROI starts to happen. But how do you make those kinds of changes and still keep the business running?

How to transform work without disrupting delivery

Deep transformation, as I’ve noted, requires more than introducing new technology. It can mean combining responsibilities, removing process steps, redefining roles and changing how teams collaborate.

That’s a big enough challenge. Now add in the stress of trying to keep the machine that is your organization humming while undertaking it. Employees and managers, after all, may be understandably reluctant to interrupt established workflows when they remain accountable for quarterly targets, service levels and ongoing delivery.

Early adopters can help by embracing experimentation. But their willingness to take risks cannot simply be replicated across the workforce through training or communication campaigns. Without practical experience and confidence, teams are likely to revert to their familiar processes, even if leadership has provided a new framework.

This is what I mean by changing the engine while flying. It’s the inherent tension between transformation and continuity. As a leader, you cannot simply suspend business operations until an ideal future state is ready. Instead, you have to create enough operational capacity to accommodate the temporary disruption that meaningful reinvention may require.

We worked with one major bank that decided to take this approach in order to completely transform their software development workflow. This was not about giving their developers new AI tools. It was about redefining roles and workflows end-to-end in the whole software development life cycle.

To take that kind of dramatic leap, they paused their work for two to four weeks to redesign processes and train the team in the new ways of working in real-world scenarios. It was a significant break, of course, but they planned for the disruption and adjusted their delivery schedule accordingly.

And when they picked things back up, they were operating with substantially greater productivity (2-4x) and were able to make up for the break while still delivering the agreed-upon quarterly results.

While a long break like that might not have been appropriate for the bank’s customer-facing operations, it was a good fit for this kind of behind-the-scenes software work. If the organization had been looking to transform a customer-facing workflow, they might have instead dedicated a small portion of capacity to transformation rather than stopping the entire function.

In both cases, however, the goal is to create room for transformation before expecting transformational results. Additional capacity gives teams room to learn new workflows, absorb temporary productivity losses and maintain essential delivery commitments while the new operating model takes shape.

Transformation requires leadership to take risks and responsibility, since only leaders have the authority to interrupt services and empower teams to rearrange roles and functions. But it also demands deliberate capacity planning, hands-on support and a willingness to accept short-term disruption for better long-term performance.

That brings leaders to their next challenge: Persuading the organization to take this risk when not everyone believes it will work.

Leading without consensus: Prove the model, build confidence, then scale

Many organizations make the same mistake: They try to transform everyone at once. Put simply, company-wide AI rollouts do not produce company-wide reinvention.

A better approach than distributing equal resources across the organization is to identify teams who are already experimenting with AI and concentrate your resources to support them as they tackle meaningful business problems. That’s how you start to build a lighthouse, or a demonstrable example of successful, deep-tissue transformation, using three essential elements:

  1. Innovators: Leaders willing to experiment and challenge established ways of working.
  2. A meaningful business problem: A challenge important enough that solving it produces measurable business value, such as lower costs, increased revenue or additional capacity for innovation.
  3. A sherpa: Someone with firsthand experience implementing this kind of transformation who can help the team navigate obstacles and build confidence.

The key to making your lighthouse shine? A demonstrated business impact, not just an impressive AI application. And teams must have enough autonomy to redesign end-to-end processes across functional boundaries, rather than scrambling for across-the-board departmental approval for every proposed change.

Once the lighthouse is sending out a clear beacon, it’s time to turn that demonstrated success into organizational momentum. A successful lighthouse, after all, provides evidence that transformation can work under the organization’s actual conditions and constraints.

With that evidence, leaders can develop a repeatable blueprint and deploy experienced practitioners to support the next wave of teams. These practitioners serve as both implementation support and credible advocates, helping colleagues navigate the risks of changing established processes.

And as successful examples accumulate, the organization can make broader structural decisions based on demonstrated results, rather than theoretical designs presented on a whiteboard. It’s a classic case of “show, don’t tell.” And it can be an incredibly powerful catalyst for transformation.

To get real AI results, change how work gets done

Plenty of organizations are using AI to make their employees faster and more productive. But is that really why people got so excited about AI in the first place? No. The greatest opportunity wasn’t about gains at the margins; it was about transformation. It was about the potential for significant productivity improvements and business transformation.

But you don’t get there by rolling out copilots and other one-off tools. You get there by rethinking how value is created for customers and redesigning how workflows support that value creation, including which steps remain necessary, which can be combined and where AI agents can fundamentally change execution.

Is that an easy fix? If it was, everyone would be doing it. It takes planning, courage and confidence. It means accepting some short-term disruption, providing additional capacity where necessary and giving transformation teams the authority and support to challenge established processes.

It also means recognizing that confidence is built through experience and evidence. Executive mandates, training sessions and ambitious transformation plans aren’t enough for this type of change. Deep-tissue transformation requires leaders to ask three big questions:

  • Where are we using AI to accelerate a process that should be fundamentally redesigned?
  • What meaningful business problem could demonstrate the value of this transformation within 12 weeks?
  • What capacity, autonomy and hands-on expertise would our team need to reinvent that process without compromising essential business delivery?

Finding those answers is how you start to fundamentally reinvent your operations while continuing to serve customers, deliver commitments and run the business.

Changing the engine while flying is difficult precisely because both objectives matter. The leadership challenge is to make them work together.

item.title: More control, fewer dependencies: Why DORA is forcing a connectivity rethink
item.description:
If a bank spread its investments across several funds, only to find they were all heavily exposed to the same company, its risk team would have some difficult questions to answer. I think it’s high time CIOs brought that same level of curiosity and skepticism to their network architecture. When we distribute applications across different providers, we need to know where their apparent “independence” actually ends.

Resilience depends on independence. That is, a plan B only works if it isn’t exposed to the same set of variables as Plan A. While a second cloud might open up more options to businesses, its value as a fallback depends entirely on whether people can still reach it if something fails. If the path to both clouds passes through the same infrastructure, a single disruption can leave customers stranded while the applications themselves keep running. That lack of business continuity is a difficult thing for a CIO and their team to explain to the board, particularly when the company has invested so much in resilience, and it’s why I believe that connectivity deserves a seat at the top table.

I’m not alone. Europe’s Digital Operational Resilience Act, or DORA, is forcing financial institutions to examine the dependencies behind their digital services, and much of that tracks back to network architecture. CIOs based in the US ought to pay attention, because the underlying exposure is just as relevant to their business. Europe, it seems, is ahead of the game. The OCC, a US federal agency that supervises national banks, recently highlighted operational resilience and third-party risk management in its Spring 2025 risk report, pointing to disruptions across financial services and other sectors. A US bank’s customers expect to reach their money regardless of where its technology suppliers are based. DORA gives CIOs a reason to look beneath their cloud strategy and ask whether the connections supporting it can deliver that continuity – “What can fail here? And what will still work when it does?”

A European regulation, a familiar American problem

What really interests me about DORA is that it asks the hard questions. Namely, how financial businesses plan to keep operating when their technology fails. Its requirements extend from managing technology risk to testing resilience, with a mandate to report major incidents while overseeing external providers. DORA is pushing institutions to examine how much their ability to serve customers depends on decisions and infrastructure largely outside of their control, and that’s what sets it apart from other regulations.

The first joint report from the European Supervisory Authorities found that 29% of major technology incidents reported across the EU financial sector in 2025 originated with third parties. Around a third had effects across borders, reflecting the shared infrastructure and services that connect financial institutions. While those figures cover a wide range of failures, they do give CIOs everywhere a fairly compelling reason to investigate where their own dependencies sit.

The first thing to consider is how suppliers are evaluated. Just because a provider boasts strong recovery processes for its own services, it doesn’t follow that they’re somehow immune from disruption. Firms need that assurance, so they need to understand where their provider’s dependencies actually sit, including at the infrastructure level. That kind of knowledge demands a conversation between the people buying services, the engineers connecting them and leaders like CIO’s who are responsible for business continuity. I’d want that conversation to follow a critical service far enough to expose the dependencies beneath it. Otherwise, we risk approving a recovery plan whose success rests on assumptions nobody has tested.

Following the dependencies beneath the cloud

Personally, I’d start with a service customers depend on, such as making a payment through an online banking app, and trace what has to work for that payment to go through. The app might run in one cloud while drawing on a fraud detection service in another and a core banking system elsewhere. Each part could have its own backup arrangements, sure, but understanding whether the payment can still proceed means we have to look a little deeper. Two connections bought from different carriers may use the same underlying fiber route. Likewise, entirely separate routes may enter a building through the same conduit, or converge at a facility that both depend on. A failure at that shared point can take away the primary connection and its backup together, so is it really a backup at all?

A CIO shouldn’t be afraid to bring this discussion into procurement, asking suppliers to explain how their proposed routes differ and what evidence supports that separation. If any of that detail is difficult to obtain, or the provider isn’t forthcoming, there’s your first red flag. Assuming the dependencies are visible, businesses can start making better decisions about where alternative connections may help. I’d prioritize the services which most closely impact customers, giving them a viable route through disruption if and when it does occur, with enough capacity to easily support those services.

Direct interconnection can help by reducing the number of networks traffic needs to cross. An Internet Exchange, or IX, brings networks together so they can exchange traffic directly. Where the relevant networks are present and agree to interconnect, traffic can follow a shorter path with fewer intermediary networks involved. Exchanging traffic locally can also avoid unnecessary journeys to distant hubs, making performance more predictable. Private cloud connectivity is also useful to consider. Through an interconnection platform, an institution can establish dedicated connections to cloud providers, giving it greater control over how traffic reaches those services. Private connections between networks and between clouds serve different needs, but both can help engineers build paths that are easier to understand and manage.

The value of adopting solutions like these lies in the choices they generate. A connection through a separate facility may provide an alternative when the primary location becomes unavailable, while physically diverse routes can reduce exposure to a single fiber cut. However, the access connections to those facilities need the same scrutiny as the infrastructure inside them. An institution can inadvertently recreate its original dependency if every route to its new interconnection platform shares the same vulnerable link. That’s why I’d judge the design through testing. If the primary connection goes down, the surviving path needs to carry the required traffic while keeping the service usable. And when I say “usable”, it’s important to remember that even a payment that eventually completes after repeated timeouts is still a serious disruption in the eyes of the customer.

I see interconnection as an opportunity to exercise greater control over the infrastructure our business depends on. An institution meeting its DORA obligations can still choose to strengthen its Internet connectivity through more independent routes and direct connections to the online services it uses, and that’s what digital sovereignty means here – having more say over how traffic travels and more options when a provider or path becomes unavailable. An IX isn’t mandated by DORA, but it can help create those options, provided the connections supporting it are designed and tested with the same care.

Giving connectivity a seat in the boardroom

So, coming full circle, a bank wouldn’t consider its investments diversified simply because it held several funds. It would examine what those funds owned and whether they shared exposure to the same company. For CIOs, choosing several providers is a start, but we need to follow their connections far enough to understand whether one failure could leave them all unreachable.

That’s why connectivity needs to enter the conversation while investment decisions are still being made. If a new cloud service is to support an essential business function, its connections belong in the discussion about how that function will survive a disruption. The cost of an independent route can then be weighed against the consequences of losing access, with business leaders involved in deciding what level of risk they’ll accept.

I believe DORA’s scrutiny gives US technology leaders a valuable opportunity to examine those choices in their own organizations. We can use it to ask better questions of suppliers and make recovery plans more credible, but ultimately, I’d want to be able to explain how a customer will still reach an essential service when its usual connection disappears. Following that question down through the architecture is where the real work begins.

item.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI
item.description:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, OpenAI's Brian Yang described building the ChatGPT ads product with Codex agents and no human-written code. He outlined layered testing, sandboxes, and batched pull request reviews, and noted failure modes such as code "slop" and unsafe agent actions. He advised gradual adoption and framed engineers as managers of agents.

By Daniel Curtis
